header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking

related.why: The next step in his pathway

brief.scenario: Mr Keith Barlow, 62, has been referred by his GP after passing blood in his urine.
brief.task: Take a focused history. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to summarise your history, then asked about differential diagnosis, investigation and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Painless visible haematuria at 62 is bladder or kidney cancer until proven otherwise.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Ask whether he is passing urine now, then open the history.

grid.label: Opening and rapport
grid.fail: Closed questions from the start, without introduction.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, asks an open question and listens.
grid.high: Uses his words ("red wine colour") and checks what he means before moving on.

grid.label: Characterising the haematuria
grid.fail: Doesn't establish that it was visible and painless.
grid.pass: Colour, painless or painful, number of episodes, clots, timing in the stream.
grid.high: Explains why timing matters: initial suggests a urethral source; terminal suggests the bladder neck or prostate; total suggests the bladder or above.

grid.label: Voiding and clot retention (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Never asks whether he can pass urine.
grid.pass: Asks about clots, difficulty passing urine and lower abdominal pain now.
grid.high: States the plan if he couldn't void: 3-way catheter, clot washout and irrigation, with bloods including clotting.

grid.label: Other causes
grid.fail: Accepts an infection explanation without asking about urinary symptoms.
grid.pass: Asks about dysuria, frequency, fever, loin pain, trauma, recent sore throat, beetroot or rifampicin.
grid.high: Explains that UTI must be excluded, and that visible haematuria persisting after treatment still needs investigation.

grid.label: Risk factors
grid.fail: Asks about smoking without quantifying it, or omits occupation.
grid.pass: Smoking in pack-years; occupation with dyes, rubber or textiles; previous pelvic radiotherapy.
grid.high: Explains the long latency of occupational exposure, so he asks about jobs decades ago.

grid.label: The anticoagulant and his concerns
grid.fail: Agrees it's the blood thinner, or tells him to stop it.
grid.pass: Explains that anticoagulants don't explain haematuria away; advises him not to stop apixaban himself.
grid.high: Explores his concern about work and names the need to rule out cancer honestly.

grid.label: Summary at the signal
grid.fail: Retells the history without a working diagnosis.
grid.pass: Concise summary with key positives and negatives; working diagnosis of bladder or renal cancer.
grid.high: Leads with risk: smoker, rubber-industry exposure, painless clots; then lists benign alternatives.

grid.label: Referral and investigation
grid.fail: Sends urine for culture only and plans GP review.
grid.pass: Meets NG12 suspected cancer criteria (45 or over, unexplained visible haematuria); arranges flexible cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging.
grid.high: Adds renal function before contrast, and that urine biomarkers don't replace cystoscopy.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: You've had blood in your water. Any stinging?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No? It might be a water infection anyway.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: You're on apixaban, so that'll be the cause. Maybe stop it for a week.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Mr Barlow has had haematuria, probably from his apixaban. I'd send an MSU and ask the GP to review.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Evans, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? Tell me what happened.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: What colour was it? Was it painful? How many times? Any clots? Was it at the start, the end, or all the way through?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Are you passing urine normally now? Any difficulty or tummy pain?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Any stinging, frequency or fever? Pain in your side? Any injury, sore throat, or beetroot? Any antibiotics like rifampicin?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: How many a day do you smoke, and for how long? What work have you done? Ever had radiotherapy to your pelvis?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The apixaban can make bleeding more obvious, but it doesn't explain it, so we still need to find the cause. Please don't stop it yourself.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mr Barlow, 62, has had two episodes of painless visible haematuria with clots over three weeks. He's voiding normally. No UTI symptoms. He has a 40 pack-year history and worked in a rubber factory, and takes apixaban. I'm concerned about bladder cancer; the differential includes renal cancer, prostate bleeding or stones.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: He meets the NG12 suspected cancer criteria: 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria, so he stays on that pathway. I'd arrange flexible cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Evans, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? First: are you able to pass urine at the moment? Good. Tell me what happened. When you say "red wine", was it dark red throughout?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Timing tells me where it's from: at the start suggests the urethra; at the end, the bladder neck or prostate; all the way through, the bladder or above.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [To examiner] If he couldn't void, I'd arrange a 3-way catheter, clot washout and irrigation, with FBC, renal function and clotting.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any stinging or fever? If an infection is found, we'd treat it, but if the blood persists afterwards you still need the tests.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That rubber factory: 25 years ago? That still matters; these chemicals can take decades to cause problems.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You were worried about time off work. The tests are quick, usually as outpatient visits. I'd be wrong not to say we need to rule out a growth in the bladder or kidney.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A 62-year-old smoker with occupational rubber exposure and painless visible haematuria with clots. He's voiding, has no UTI features, and his apixaban doesn't explain it. Bladder cancer is my main concern, then renal or upper-tract tumour; benign causes are prostate bleeding and stones.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He stays on the suspected cancer pathway. I'd arrange flexible cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging, ultrasound or CT urogram by local protocol, with renal function checked before contrast. A urine biomarker wouldn't replace cystoscopy.

failures.move: Not asking whether he can pass urine.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: misses clot retention, which needs a 3-way catheter, washout and irrigation now.

failures.move: Attributing the bleeding to apixaban, or advising him to stop it.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: delays a cancer diagnosis and exposes him to stroke risk from unplanned anticoagulant withdrawal.

failures.move: Asking only about his current job.
failures.consequence: Misses a past occupational exposure that raises his risk.

recovery.when: You forgot to ask about voiding
recovery.line: Before we go on: are you able to pass urine normally now?

recovery.when: He asks if it's the blood thinner
recovery.line: It can make bleeding more noticeable, but we still need to find where it's coming from.

knowledge.fact: NG12 suspected cancer pathway criteria for bladder and renal cancer: 45+ with unexplained visible haematuria without UTI, or persisting or recurring after UTI treatment (1.6.4, 1.6.6).
Any single episode of visible haematuria is significant; do not attribute it to anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.
Clot retention: 3-way catheter, washout, irrigation; assess anticoagulation.
About half of UK bladder cancers are caused by smoking; dye, rubber and textile chemicals take 30 to 40+ years.

recall.think: Bladder or renal cancer; clot retention.
recall.say: "Painless visible haematuria: cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging on the suspected cancer pathway."
do: Ask: can you pass urine now?
Don't blame or stop the anticoagulant

numbers.meaning: unexplained visible haematuria: suspected cancer criteria

recall.trap: "He's on apixaban, so that explains it."

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9-minute stations with 1 minute's reading; introduce yourself and confirm identity at every station

sources.name: NICE NG12: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral
sources.supports: Suspected cancer pathway criteria for bladder cancer (1.6.4) and renal cancer (1.6.6) at 45+ with unexplained visible haematuria

sources.name: Renal Association and BAUS: Joint consensus statement on the initial assessment of haematuria
sources.supports: Any single episode of visible haematuria is significant; exclude UTI and transient causes; haematuria should not be attributed to anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy; pseudo-haematuria (beetroot, rifampicin); all visible haematuria referred to urology

sources.name: GIRFT Urology: Urgent and emergency care and SDEC pathways (emergency haematuria pathway)
sources.supports: Unable to void: 3-way urethral catheter, washout of clots, irrigation; assess anticoagulation; imaging by ultrasound or CT urogram per local policy; investigate on the Faster Diagnosis Standard pathway

sources.name: NICE NG2: Bladder cancer: diagnosis and management
sources.version: Published 25 February 2015; minor changes, latest April 2026
sources.supports: Do not substitute urinary biomarkers for cystoscopy (1.2.1)

sources.name: Cancer Research UK: Bladder cancer risks and causes
sources.version: Web page dated 6 August 2026 (next update due August 2029)
sources.supports: About half of UK bladder cancers caused by smoking; workplace chemicals (dyes, rubber, textiles) with a latency of 30 to 40 years or more

partner.opening: Please take a focused history from Mr Barlow. I'll stop you at 6 minutes to summarise.
partner.actorBrief: You are Keith Barlow, 62, a delivery driver. Opening line: "I've been passing blood. The GP says it's probably my blood thinner." Emotional state: keen to play it down. Volunteer only that your urine looked "like red wine" twice. Release the other facts only when asked (see reveals). Hidden concern: you are self-employed and can't afford time off; say so only if asked what worries you. Idea: it's the apixaban. Expectation: to be told to stop the apixaban.

reveals.trigger: Asks about pain, episodes, clots, timing
reveals.finding: Painless; two episodes over three weeks; small clots once; red all the way through. Clear since.

reveals.trigger: Asks whether he can pass urine now
reveals.finding: "Yes, fine now." No lower abdominal pain.

reveals.trigger: Asks about urinary symptoms, fever, loin pain, trauma, diet, drugs
reveals.finding: Gets up once at night; no stinging, fever, loin pain or injury; no beetroot; no rifampicin.
20 a day for 40 years; still smokes.
Worked in a tyre and rubber factory for 12 years, until 25 years ago.
Apixaban for atrial fibrillation, started 6 months ago; ramipril.
"I'm self-employed. If I'm off, I don't get paid."
Say: "Please stop there and summarise your history."

push.question: What is your differential?
push.expect: Bladder cancer; renal or upper-tract tumour; prostate bleeding; stones; UTI.

push.question: How would you investigate him?
push.expect: Meets NG12 suspected cancer criteria (45+); candidate arranges flexible cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging.

push.question: Should he stop his apixaban?
push.expect: Not on his own; the anticoagulant doesn't explain the bleeding.

curveballs.prompt: He says he hasn't passed urine for 8 hours and his lower tummy hurts.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Clot retention: 3-way catheter, washout, irrigation, bloods including clotting; admit.

curveballs.prompt: His GP's urine dip showed nitrites and leucocytes.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Treat the infection, but investigate if haematuria persists or recurs afterwards.

curveballs.prompt: "Can't I just have a urine test instead of the camera?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Urine tests don't replace cystoscopy, which is how we look inside the bladder.
